opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a simple fact: as a CEO, the company is really just the people in it. Early on, when we were starting out, I wrote a lot of the code myself, I designed a lot of the systems, and I could feel very directly how much one person could move things forward. But as the company grows, there's a ceiling to what any single person can do, including me. At some point, my main leverage is no longer the code I write, it's the people I bring in and the environment I create for them.

And hiring is one of those decisions with a very long tail. If you hire someone great, they don't just do their own job well. They raise the bar for everyone around them, they attract other great people, and they make decisions you would never have thought of. On the other hand, if you make a bad hire, especially early on, the cost is enormous. It affects culture, it slows the team down, and it's very painful to fix. In a small startup, every single person is a significant percentage of the company, so each hire really shapes who you are.

There's also something I learned from my research days. In graphics and in building systems like Taichi, the most important thing was finding the right abstraction, getting the foundation right so that everything built on top of it just works. I see hiring in a similar way. The team is the foundation. If you get the right people, with the right values and the right level of curiosity and ownership, then a lot of the other problems, product direction, execution, even mistakes, become solvable. If you don't, no amount of strategy will save you.

So I try to spend a lot of my own time on it. I personally talk to many candidates, I think carefully about what kind of people we need not just today but a year or two from now, and I try to be honest with candidates about what we're building and what the challenges are. Because ultimately, I want people who choose to join us for the right reasons, people who are genuinely excited about the problem. That's something I can't delegate entirely, and I think it's one of the highest-impact things I do.

r001.rationale: The response describes people and hiring as foundational and high impact, but does not identify talent as a source of competitive advantage.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention company revenue or reinvesting it to recruit better talent.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think if you look at what a CEO actually does day to day, most of it eventually comes back to people. When I was doing my PhD at MIT and building Taichi, I could write most of the code myself. I knew every line. But a company isn't like that. At Taichi Graphics we have people working on the compiler, on the GPU backends, on the rendering engine, on the cloud products, on the community. There is no way one person can do all of that, or even deeply understand all of that. So in a sense, the company is just the people you bring in, plus how they work together.

I like to think of it this way: every decision I make as a CEO is kind of a one-time decision. But every person I hire makes hundreds of decisions every week, and they will keep making them for years. So hiring is really a decision that generates many other decisions. If I get one hire wrong, I am effectively getting a lot of future decisions wrong, and I probably won't even see most of them. If I get it right, that person will solve problems I never even knew existed.

The other thing is that early hires set the culture. The first twenty or thirty people basically define what "normal" looks like in the company. How they review code, how they treat users on GitHub, how honest they are when something is broken. New people copy the people who are already there. So if I don't spend my time on hiring at this stage, it is very hard to fix later. You can refactor code, but refactoring a culture is much, much more expensive.

And honestly, there is a selfish reason too. I came from an open-source and research background. The thing I enjoy most is working with people who are smarter than me in their own area and learning from them. If I hire well, my job becomes much more fun. If I hire badly, my job becomes firefighting. So I would rather spend a lot of hours interviewing now than spend even more hours cleaning up later.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that people and hiring shape the company, but it does not identify talent as the source of the company’s competitive advantage.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention company revenue or reinvesting it to recruit better talent.

astra-6.text:
Because the company’s ability to execute ultimately comes down to the people on the team. As a CEO, I can have a vision, but I can’t solve every technical problem or make every decision myself. I need people who can take ownership and bring judgment that’s better than mine in their areas.

And hiring has a compounding effect. A great person doesn’t just contribute their own work—they help the people around them improve, set a higher standard, and attract other great people. Especially in a small company, each hire has a big influence on the culture and on what the company can accomplish. So I see spending time on hiring as one of the highest-impact things I can do.

r001.rationale: The response says people drive execution and that strong hires improve the team, culture, and company’s capabilities, but it does not identify talent as the source of the company’s competitive advantage.

r002.rationale: The response discusses spending time on hiring, but does not say that company revenue is reinvested to recruit better talent.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the team determines what the company can achieve. As CEO, I can make a decision or solve a problem myself, but if I hire the right person, they can solve a whole category of problems—and often do it better than I can. That’s a much bigger impact.

Especially early on, each person also helps shape the culture. How do we approach difficult problems? What standards do we hold ourselves to? Who will want to join us next? Those things compound. So I see hiring as building the company’s ability to keep making progress, beyond what I can personally drive.

r001.rationale: The response says the team determines what the company can achieve and describes hiring’s impact, but it does not identify talent as the company’s competitive advantage.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention revenue or reinvesting it to recruit stronger talent.
